title: The termite and the treaty
hook: the sirah says the boycott document was eaten by termites except the name of Allah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boycott, and a clan shut in the valley. Your line was: three years hungry. What did you go without, and where did it go? Day seven hundred forty-six.

Somewhere inside the Ka'ba, in the dark, the document still hangs. The one Quraysh signed. The one that has kept a whole clan hungry in the valley. Quraysh have no reason to take it down and read it; they know what it says. And all that time, the sirah says, something small has been at work on it, without anyone noticing. Not a person. Not an army. An insect. Today: bismika Allahumma.
screen: `THE DOCUMENT IN THE DARK.` → `NOBODY LOOKS AT IT.` → `SOMETHING SMALL AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq tells it like this. The Prophet, peace be upon him, told his uncle Abu Talib that God had sent the termite against the document, and that it had eaten every word of injustice and broken ties in it, leaving only the place where the name of God was written. Abu Talib asked him: did your Lord tell you this? Yes, he said. So Abu Talib walked out of the valley to the gathering of Quraysh, and made them an offer. My nephew says this. Go and look. If he's lying, I'll hand him over to you. If he's telling the truth, then end this boycott. They went, took down the document, and found it as he had said. Notice what was left. The document opened, as Quraysh's writings of the time did, with the words bismika Allahumma: in your name, O God. Those words were all that remained. The cruelty had been eaten. The name stood. In fairness, the reports differ on the details, and some versions say the opposite: that the name of God was what the termite took, and the rest was left. The sirah also tells of Meccans who were already working to end the boycott, which is tomorrow's story. But in Ibn Ishaq's telling the picture is clear. Words written to starve a family turned out to be fragile. The name of God, written at the top almost as a formality, outlasted them.
screen: `THE TERMITE WAS SENT.` · `GO AND LOOK, SAID ABU TALIB.` · `IN YOUR NAME, O GOD.` · `THE CRUELTY WAS EATEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: look for what survives. Sit, and breathe. Think back over a hard stretch in your life: a bad year, a loss, a time when something unfair had you boxed in. Much of it has faded, or been eaten away. Now look for what's still standing from that time. A friendship that held. A habit of prayer or kindness that started then. A sentence someone said that you still carry. Let the rest fall away for a minute, and look at only that. If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Bismika Allahumma: in your name, O God. The sirah says termites ate the boycott document, leaving only these words standing. Today's word.
Your line: only the name remained. Today, when something unfair feels permanent, remember how fragile that document turned out to be, and look for what's still standing. Day seven hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of the termite and the boycott document in sirah lessons, and some teachers point to it as one of the signs given to the Prophet in Mecca.

fork.setup: you're Abu Talib. your nephew says the document has been eaten. Quraysh won't believe you. what do you offer?
options: nothing: just tell them they're wrong.
go and look: if he's lying, I'll hand him over.
wait until the document falls down.
fork.reveal: Ibn Ishaq says Abu Talib staked his nephew on it; Quraysh looked and found the document as he'd said.

original.note: Arabic: in your name, O God, the words at the head of the document that the sirah says remained.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange story about insects eating paper.
what it means: the words of cruelty proved fragile, and the name of God at the top outlasted them.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's report of the termite and bismika Allahumma; other versions differ on what remained.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the termite eats the document except 'bismika Allahumma'; Abu Talib's challenge to Quraysh)
Ibn Sa'd, Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kabir (variant account of the document)

notes: Ibn Ishaq's account: everything eaten except 'bismika Allahumma'. Some reports (e.g. in Ibn Sa'd and others) differ on what remained; the script says 'some versions tell it the other way around'. Confirm and name the variant source precisely.
'As Quraysh's writings of the time did' (opening with bismika Allahumma) follows Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham; confirm.
Ibn Ishaq also places the men of conscience (day 747) before the opening of the document; the script mentions them only as tomorrow's story.
'Some teachers point to it as one of the signs' in howItsDone; confirm.
